screens.title: Mastering Continuous Delivery: Automated Staging Deployments
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we move from continuous integration to continuous delivery, focusing on automated staging deployments. You will learn why staging matters: it is a near-production environment where the exact artifact built in CI is validated through user acceptance, performance and security checks. We will show how to retrieve the same build artifact from an artifact repository, provision staging infrastructure with Infrastructure as Code, and inject environment-specific configuration and secrets at deployment time. You will also see how manual approval gates act as a final human checkpoint before production. A concrete example runs through pulling a Docker image tagged in CI and deploying it to a Kubernetes staging cluster using a manifest and kubectl. Common pitfalls such as hardcoding configuration, environment drift, and missing rollback plans will be highlighted with practical mitigations. By the end you should be able to design a CD pipeline that deploys the exact CI artifact into a reproducible staging environment, validates it, and pauses for a controlled release decision. Consider how your team would use a staging environment to reduce surprises in production.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Mastering Continuous Delivery
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Mastering Continuous Delivery

Prepare build artifacts, provision staging with IaC, inject environment configuration, and gate releases with human approvals.

In this lesson
Design an automated staging deployment pipeline that reuses CI artifacts.
Coming up
IaC provisioning, Kubernetes manifests, and secret injection patterns.
Hands-on
Deploy a Docker image to a local Kubernetes staging cluster using kubectl.
Why this chapter matters

Staging is the final automated stop before production. Using the exact artifact and scripted infrastructure reduces surprises, improves repeatability, and keeps sensitive data out of code. Manual approval gates let teams balance automation with business oversight.

Example
A Docker image tagged in CI is pulled by the CD pipeline and deployed unchanged to staging for UAT.
Common risk
Hardcoded configs or missing rollback plans can turn staging validation into production outages.
Pipeline Snapshot
CI → Artifact Repo → CD to Staging → Tests → Manual Approval → Production
The visual shows the flow you will design: a single artifact built once and deployed many times, combined with scripted staging infrastructure and a final manual gate.
Explore Key Topics
Build Once, Deploy Many
Use the identical build artifact across environments to avoid inconsistencies.
Infrastructure as Code
Script staging provisioning so environments are reproducible and versioned.
Approval Gates
Add a human checkpoint for release timing and final reviews.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: Throughout this chapter you will acquire four practical skills that let you design and operate a staging deployment workflow. First, you will design and implement an automated deployment process to a staging environment so changes that pass CI can be exercised safely before production. For example, you will script kubectl apply steps that deploy the exact image built in CI. Second, you will identify how artifact repositories store the build output and how a CD pipeline fetches that artifact rather than rebuilding. This avoids subtle differences between environments. Third, you will apply Infrastructure as Code principles to define and recreate staging infrastructure reliably; version-controlled templates let teams reproduce clusters, networks, and services. Fourth, you will configure environment-specific variables and secrets so sensitive values are injected during deployment, and you will add manual approval gates to your pipeline to allow final human review. Each objective includes a competency milestone so you can verify that the pipeline works end to end and a staging deploy can be approved for production.

screens.title: What is Continuous Delivery for staging?
screens.narratorSegment: Continuous Delivery is the automation of preparing a build for release so that every change which passes Continuous Integration is ready to be deployed to a target environment. In practice, this means the CD pipeline takes the artifact proven by CI and applies scripted deployment steps to a staging or pre-production environment where further validation happens. The staging environment exists to mirror production closely and serve as the last automated and manual testing ground, including user acceptance, performance, and security checks. A concrete example is a Docker image tagged by CI: instead of rebuilding, the CD pipeline pulls my_app:v1.2.3-abcd123 from a registry and deploys it to staging for verification. A common misconception is that CD automatically means anything goes to production; in fact, CD emphasizes readiness and repeatability while leaving a deliberate manual gate for final release decisions. The key takeaway is that Continuous Delivery reduces risk by ensuring the same artifact is exercised in a realistic environment before a human approves production release. How would you describe the difference between a passing CI build and a CD-ready artifact in your team?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › What is Continuous Delivery?
Core Concept

Continuous Delivery for staging

CD takes the CI-built artifact and deploys it to a realistic staging environment for further validation, preserving artifact identity and environment parity.

Why it matters
It reduces surprises by validating the exact artifact in a mirror of production before any manual release decision.
Concrete example
A Docker image built in CI is pulled unchanged into staging for UAT and security scans.
Misconception
Continuous Delivery does not remove the need for a manual approval gate; it ensures readiness and repeatability before that gate.
Analogy
Think of CI as baking a cake and CD as packaging that same cake in a sealed box for tasting in a test kitchen. You never bake a new cake for each tasting; you use the same box to guarantee feedback applies to the original product.
Key Takeaway
Key Takeaway

Use the exact CI artifact in staging. CD ensures the artifact is ready for release and stage tests will reflect production behavior.

screens.title: Build Artifacts and the "Build Once, Deploy Many" principle
screens.narratorSegment: The 'Build Once, Deploy Many' principle means the exact artifact created and tested in CI is the artifact deployed across staging and production environments. This avoids differences that can occur when rebuilding for each target. A concrete example: your CI creates a Docker image tagged my_app:v1.2.3-abcd123 and stores it in an artifact registry. The CD pipeline pulls that exact tag and deploys it to staging. If the pipeline instead rebuilt the image at deploy time, small changes in build tools or environment could introduce new bugs. A common mistake is to rely on mutable tags like 'latest' without capturing the digest; this risks deploying a different binary than the one tested. Practical checks include verifying image digests and referencing immutable tags, and ensuring your CD job fetches artifacts from a secure registry. The takeaway is straightforward: keep artifacts immutable between CI and staging so tests in staging truly validate the CI output. Build Artifacts and the "Build Once, Deploy Many" principle means always deploy the immutable artifact produced by ci to ensure staging and production run identical software.. In practical terms, why retrieving the exact artifact is essential for consistency. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Build Once, Deploy Many
Definition

Build once, deploy many

Use the exact artifact produced by CI for all deployments to guarantee consistency across staging and production.

Concrete example
A Docker image my_app:v1.2.3-abcd123 built in CI is pulled unchanged by CD and deployed to staging.
Common mistake
Rebuilding at deploy time can introduce tool or dependency differences and obscure whether CI tests actually validated the deployed artifact.
Practical checks
  • Pin artifact tags or use digests to reference immutable builds.
  • Store artifacts in a secure registry and fetch them in CD steps rather than rebuilding.
  • Log artifact identifiers in release notes so traceability is clear.
Key Takeaway

Immutable artifacts are the single source of truth across environments; deploy them unchanged to preserve test validity.

screens.title: Fetching artifacts: registry and pull commands
screens.narratorSegment: Retrieving the exact artifact is a simple but crucial step in any CD pipeline. In many containerized workflows the CD job runs a registry pull using the tag or digest created in CI. For example, the pipeline might execute a command to pull myregistry. com/my_app:v1.2.3-abcd123 and then deploy that image. The key is to reference the immutable identifier produced by CI. A common misconception is that using a floating tag like latest is safe because it points to the newest validated image; in practice it can point to an untested image if tagging is not coordinated. Always pass the artifact identifier from CI to CD as a parameter. In this walkthrough you will see an example pull command and how to embed it into a deploy job. After pulling, the pipeline should verify the image digest and proceed to deployment only if the digest matches the CI record. This ensures the artifact pulled into staging is exactly what CI tested. Fetching artifacts: registry and pull commands means cd must pull the immutable artifact identifier produced by ci and verify its identity before deploying to staging.. In practical terms, how cd retrieves the exact artifact produced by ci. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Fetching artifacts
Code Walkthrough

Pull the exact image produced by CI

# Example: Pulling a Docker image from a registry in a CD pipeline
docker pull myregistry.com/my_app:v1.2.3-abcd123

# Verify digest matches the CI-recorded digest
docker inspect --format='{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' myregistry.com/my_app:v1.2.3-abcd123
Use the exact tag or digest passed from CI. Do not rely on mutable tags or local rebuilds when deploying to staging.
Practical notes
  • Pass artifact identifiers from CI to CD via pipeline variables or build metadata.
  • Verify the pulled artifact digest against the CI-recorded digest before deployment.
  • Use secure access to the registry with credentials stored in secret managers.
Key Takeaway

Treat the registry pull and digest check as the trust boundary between CI and CD. If they don't match, stop the deploy.

screens.title: Infrastructure as Code for staging environments
screens.narratorSegment: Infrastructure as Code is the practice of describing your infrastructure in machine-readable files so it can be provisioned, updated, and torn down programmatically. For staging this means using Terraform, Ansible, or cloud templates to create clusters, networks, and services that mirror production. A concrete scenario: an IaC template provisions a Kubernetes cluster and networking, then the CD pipeline applies manifests to deploy the application image. The advantage is reproducibility and version control — teams can track changes to environment definitions and roll back if a template causes issues. A common misconception is that IaC automatically guarantees identical hardware; IaC guarantees the same configuration, but cloud provider differences or quota limits can still cause differences. To reduce drift, include declarative resource definitions and automated validation steps after provisioning. The takeaway is that IaC converts environment management into code, enabling consistent staging environments that you can recreate, test, and audit. Infrastructure as Code for staging environments means use iac to define, version, and provision staging resources so environments are reproducible and auditable.. In practical terms, provisioning repeatable staging using iac tools. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Infrastructure as Code
Architecture

IaC for staging

Define clusters, networks, and managed services in version-controlled templates and let the CD pipeline provision them automatically.
Example flow
IaC creates the cluster; CD applies Kubernetes manifests which deploy the CI-built image to the provisioned staging cluster.
Why it matters
Reproducible environments reduce 'works on my machine' and make audits and rollbacks possible.
Drift & validation
After provisioning, run automated validation checks such as service health, namespace presence, and sample test requests to confirm the environment matches expectations.
Practice
Keep IaC in source control, review changes, and use CI to plan and test infrastructure updates before applying them to staging.
Key Takeaway

IaC makes staging reproducible and auditable; combine it with validation to detect drift before deployments run tests or manual reviews.

screens.title: Kubernetes staging manifest walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: Kubernetes manifests are a common way to deploy containerized applications into staging clusters. The manifest defines the deployment name, replicas, labels, container image, ports, and environment variables or secret references. In the example you will see a deployment named my-app-staging that uses the CI-built image myregistry. com/my_app:v1.2.3-abcd123, sets an environment variable for the staging database URL, and references a Kubernetes Secret for an A P I key. A common error is to place secret values directly in the manifest or the image; instead, reference secrets by name so they are managed separately. When deploying, the CD pipeline should apply the manifest and then run health and readiness checks. If any checks fail, the pipeline should halt and notify stakeholders. This manifest demonstrates how to keep configuration declarative and environment-specific while preserving secret separation. Kubernetes staging manifest walkthrough means kubernetes manifests specify deployment details and should reference secrets for sensitive values rather than embedding them.. In practical terms, a concrete kubernetes deployment for a staging environment. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Kubernetes manifest
Manifest snippet
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: my-app-staging
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: my-app
      env: staging
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: my-app
        env: staging
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: my-app
        image: myregistry.com/my_app:v1.2.3-abcd123 # Pulled artifact
        ports:
        - containerPort: 5000
        env:
        - name: DATABASE_URL
          value: "jdbc:postgresql://staging-db:5432/myapp"
        - name: API_KEY
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: my-app-secrets-staging
              key: api-key
Notice secrets are referenced and not inlined. The image uses the CI-provided tag so staging runs the tested artifact.
Deployment checklist
  • Confirm the image tag or digest matches CI metadata.
  • Validate secret references resolve in the cluster before creating pods.
  • Run readiness and liveness checks after apply to ensure health.
Key Takeaway

Keep manifests declarative, reference secrets, and deploy the CI artifact unchanged so staging validation is meaningful.

screens.title: Deploying with kubectl and local image policies
screens.narratorSegment: Deploying to a staging cluster typically involves applying your Kubernetes manifests with kubectl. In local environments you often use images built on the same machine, so imagePullPolicy: Never is used to tell the cluster not to pull from a registry. For cloud staging you usually pull from a registry. A concrete example is running kubectl apply -f my-app-staging. yaml after ensuring the image tag is correct. The deployment sequence is: ensure the cluster exists (IaC), ensure the secret references exist, apply the manifest, then observe pods and services with kubectl get commands. A common misconception is that imagePullPolicy Never is unsafe—it's appropriate for local workflows where you control the image build, but for shared staging you should push to a registry and use immutable tags. After applying manifests, use readiness probes and kubectl get pods to validate the deployment. If pods fail, do not proceed to approval; fix issues and redeploy the same artifact. The takeaway: choose the right imagePullPolicy for your environment and always validate after apply. Deploying with kubectl and local image policies means use kubectl apply to deploy manifests and choose image pull policies appropriate for local versus shared staging clusters.. In practical terms, apply manifests and understand imagepullpolicy implications. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › kubectl & image policies
Process Flow

Apply, validate, observe

1. Ensure cluster
Provision staging via IaC and confirm cluster access.
2. Apply manifests
kubectl apply -f my-app-staging.yaml to create deployment and service.
3. Validate
kubectl get pods/services and check readiness and health probes before proceeding.
Local note: imagePullPolicy: Never lets you use locally built images without pushing to a registry. For shared staging, push images and reference immutable tags.
Commands reference
# Apply the manifest
kubectl apply -f my-app-staging.yaml

# Check deployments and pods
kubectl get deployments -l env=staging
kubectl get pods -l env=staging
Key Takeaway

After applying manifests, always validate environment health before moving to approval. Select imagePullPolicy based on where your image lives.

screens.title: Environment-specific configuration vs secrets
screens.narratorSegment: Applications require environment-specific configuration such as database URLs and feature flags, plus sensitive secrets like A P I keys. The recommended approach is to inject non-sensitive variables and secrets at deployment time instead of baking them into images. For example, set DATABASE_URL to point at staging-db for the staging deploy and use a secret reference for API_KEY. A common misconception is to store secrets in plain environment variables in source control; this is insecure and brittle. Better options include Kubernetes Secrets, HashiCorp Vault, or cloud secret managers and mounting or referencing them in manifests. screens.title: Manual approval gates in the CD pipeline
screens.narratorSegment: Manual approval gates are intentional pauses in a CD pipeline where designated people or teams approve progression to production. Their purpose is to allow business decisions, final quality checks, or strategic timing of releases that automation cannot reason about. For example, after a successful staging deployment and all automated tests, a product manager or release lead reviews UAT results and approves the pipeline to continue. A common misunderstanding is that approval gates slow down delivery unnecessarily; when used wisely they balance speed with accountability and reduce the risk of business-impacting releases. In practice, most CI/CD platforms support configurable approval steps tied to groups, with notifications and audit trails. Implement gates so they do not block emergency rollbacks or critical fixes; allow a controlled override workflow. The takeaway is to use manual gates as a safety mechanism that complements, not replaces, robust automated testing and observability in staging. screens.title: Common mistakes and safety notes
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson enumerates common mistakes that teams make when implementing staging deployments and offers practical mitigations. First, inconsistent environments: without IaC or containerization staging drifts from production. Mitigation: use IaC and container images to ensure parity. Second, hardcoding configurations: embedding environment-specific values in code or images creates security and flexibility problems. Mitigation: inject configurations and use secret managers. Third, neglecting staging tests: treating staging as a checkbox misses real issues; mitigate by running UAT, performance, and security scans in staging. Fourth, lack of rollback strategy: not having an automated reversal plan can turn a failed deployment into an outage; mitigate by keeping previous artifacts and scripted rollbacks. Fifth, insufficient monitoring: if you cannot observe health metrics in staging you cannot decide to release safely; add monitoring and alerts. A misconception is that adding all safeguards slows teams down—properly automated checks speed decision-making by increasing confidence. The takeaway is to include replication, secret management, validation, rollback, and monitoring in your staging pipeline. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we move from continuous integration to continuous delivery, focusing on automated staging deployments. You will learn why staging matters: it is a near-production environment where the exact artifact built in CI is validated through user acceptance, performance and security checks. We will show how to retrieve the same build artifact from an artifact repository, provision staging infrastructure with Infrastructure as Code, and inject environment-specific configuration and secrets at deployment time. You will also see how manual approval gates act as a final human checkpoint before production. A concrete example runs through pulling a Docker image tagged in CI and deploying it to a Kubernetes staging cluster using a manifest and kubectl. Common pitfalls such as hardcoding configuration, environment drift, and missing rollback plans will be highlighted with practical mitigations. By the end you should be able to design a CD pipeline that deploys the exact CI artifact into a reproducible staging environment, validates it, and pauses for a controlled release decision. Consider how your team would use a staging environment to reduce surprises in production.

Throughout this chapter you will acquire four practical skills that let you design and operate a staging deployment workflow. First, you will design and implement an automated deployment process to a staging environment so changes that pass CI can be exercised safely before production. For example, you will script kubectl apply steps that deploy the exact image built in CI. Second, you will identify how artifact repositories store the build output and how a CD pipeline fetches that artifact rather than rebuilding. This avoids subtle differences between environments. Third, you will apply Infrastructure as Code principles to define and recreate staging infrastructure reliably; version-controlled templates let teams reproduce clusters, networks, and services. Fourth, you will configure environment-specific variables and secrets so sensitive values are injected during deployment, and you will add manual approval gates to your pipeline to allow final human review. Each objective includes a competency milestone so you can verify that the pipeline works end to end and a staging deploy can be approved for production.

This second objectives screen outlines practical verification steps and why they matter. For artifact reuse, verify the pipeline pulls the identical image or artifact tag produced by CI; check the image digest or exact tag to guarantee parity. For IaC, validate that your staging environment can be destroyed and reprovisioned from code with the same results; use version control to review changes. For configuration and secrets, test that sensitive values are not baked into images by attempting a deploy with missing or rotated secrets and confirming failure modes are safe. For approval gates, confirm the manual step pauses the pipeline and notifies the right stakeholders, then test a rollback after an approval to ensure reversibility. These verification checks prevent common mistakes such as environment drift, hardcoded credentials, or unstoppable deployments, and they let you trust the staging validation process as you approach production releases.

Continuous Delivery is the automation of preparing a build for release so that every change which passes Continuous Integration is ready to be deployed to a target environment. In practice, this means the CD pipeline takes the artifact proven by CI and applies scripted deployment steps to a staging or pre-production environment where further validation happens. The staging environment exists to mirror production closely and serve as the last automated and manual testing ground, including user acceptance, performance, and security checks. A concrete example is a Docker image tagged by CI: instead of rebuilding, the CD pipeline pulls my_app:v1.2.3-abcd123 from a registry and deploys it to staging for verification. A common misconception is that CD automatically means anything goes to production; in fact, CD emphasizes readiness and repeatability while leaving a deliberate manual gate for final release decisions. The key takeaway is that Continuous Delivery reduces risk by ensuring the same artifact is exercised in a realistic environment before a human approves production release. How would you describe the difference between a passing CI build and a CD-ready artifact in your team?

The 'Build Once, Deploy Many' principle means the exact artifact created and tested in CI is the artifact deployed across staging and production environments. This avoids differences that can occur when rebuilding for each target. A concrete example: your CI creates a Docker image tagged my_app:v1.2.3-abcd123 and stores it in an artifact registry. The CD pipeline pulls that exact tag and deploys it to staging. If the pipeline instead rebuilt the image at deploy time, small changes in build tools or environment could introduce new bugs. A common mistake is to rely on mutable tags like 'latest' without capturing the digest; this risks deploying a different binary than the one tested. Practical checks include verifying image digests and referencing immutable tags, and ensuring your CD job fetches artifacts from a secure registry. The takeaway is straightforward: keep artifacts immutable between CI and staging so tests in staging truly validate the CI output. Build Artifacts and the "Build Once, Deploy Many" principle means always deploy the immutable artifact produced by ci to ensure staging and production run identical software.. In practical terms, why retrieving the exact artifact is essential for consistency. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Retrieving the exact artifact is a simple but crucial step in any CD pipeline. In many containerized workflows the CD job runs a registry pull using the tag or digest created in CI. For example, the pipeline might execute a command to pull myregistry. com/my_app:v1.2.3-abcd123 and then deploy that image. The key is to reference the immutable identifier produced by CI. A common misconception is that using a floating tag like latest is safe because it points to the newest validated image; in practice it can point to an untested image if tagging is not coordinated. Always pass the artifact identifier from CI to CD as a parameter. In this walkthrough you will see an example pull command and how to embed it into a deploy job. After pulling, the pipeline should verify the image digest and proceed to deployment only if the digest matches the CI record. This ensures the artifact pulled into staging is exactly what CI tested. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Infrastructure as Code is the practice of describing your infrastructure in machine-readable files so it can be provisioned, updated, and torn down programmatically. For staging this means using Terraform, Ansible, or cloud templates to create clusters, networks, and services that mirror production. A concrete scenario: an IaC template provisions a Kubernetes cluster and networking, then the CD pipeline applies manifests to deploy the application image. The advantage is reproducibility and version control — teams can track changes to environment definitions and roll back if a template causes issues. A common misconception is that IaC automatically guarantees identical hardware; IaC guarantees the same configuration, but cloud provider differences or quota limits can still cause differences. To reduce drift, include declarative resource definitions and automated validation steps after provisioning. The takeaway is that IaC converts environment management into code, enabling consistent staging environments that you can recreate, test, and audit. This lesson enumerates common mistakes that teams make when implementing staging deployments and offers practical mitigations. First, inconsistent environments: without IaC or containerization staging drifts from production. Mitigation: use IaC and container images to ensure parity. Second, hardcoding configurations: embedding environment-specific values in code or images creates security and flexibility problems. Mitigation: inject configurations and use secret managers. Third, neglecting staging tests: treating staging as a checkbox misses real issues; mitigate by running UAT, performance, and security scans in staging. Fourth, lack of rollback strategy: not having an automated reversal plan can turn a failed deployment into an outage; mitigate by keeping previous artifacts and scripted rollbacks. Fifth, insufficient monitoring: if you cannot observe health metrics in staging you cannot decide to release safely; add monitoring and alerts. A misconception is that adding all safeguards slows teams down—properly automated checks speed decision-making by increasing confidence. The takeaway is to include replication, secret management, validation, rollback, and monitoring in your staging pipeline.
